in_context.text: Paul has just said the gospel was entrusted to him (1:11). He now breaks into thanks to Christ for strengthening him and putting him into service, even though he was once a blasphemer and persecutor (1:13).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in Paul's name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and "own son in the faith," left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: Paul himself is the subject. He presents his own story of receiving mercy as a pattern for future believers.

what.text: Paul thanks Christ Jesus for three things. Christ gave him strength, judged him trustworthy, and appointed him to service in the ministry.

events.text: The verse looks back on Paul's change from persecutor to servant of Christ (1:13). Acts 9:22 describes Saul growing "in strength" at Damascus soon after.

written.text: Traditional: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The letter goes to Timothy in Ephesus, a wealthy port and capital of the province of Asia. Where Paul wrote from is not stated, though he had gone on to Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul is warning Timothy against false teachers who want to be teachers of the law (1:7). He sets his own story of grace beside them, showing where true ministry comes from.

big_picture.text: The passage builds toward the saying that "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief" (1:15). Paul's call to service shows mercy and longsuffering shown to the worst.

for_readers.text: Ministry is pictured as something given and empowered by Christ, not earned. Elsewhere Paul likewise says he has this ministry because he "received mercy."

why_it_matters.text: The word means "to make strong, strengthen." Paul is not saying Christ merely permitted him to serve. He says Christ gave him the strength to do it, as in Philippians 4:13 and 2 Timothy 4:17.
Here it means trusty, someone who can be trusted. That fits the idea of the gospel being "committed to my trust" (1:11).
The verb here is rendered "he esteemed." Christ is the one who judged Paul trustworthy. Paul does not claim this about himself.
The word means service, the work of a servant. It is used even of household duties. Paul describes his calling as service rather than status.

takeaway.text: Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him, trusting him, and appointing him to serve, though he had been a persecutor. His point is that ministry rests on Christ's mercy and power, not on a person's past.

unsupported.reason: The lexicon defines the word as 'the office and work of a διάκονος, service, ministry.' It does not support the contrast 'service rather than status,' and it even includes 'office.' That contrast is the card's own interpretation.
